formulas.name: FORMULA SET 2
formulas.latex: MODES OF EXISTENCE — HUNTING-GATHERING, PASTORAL, AGRICULTURAL, INDUSTRIAL

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Four modes of human existence characterised by energy source, technology, settlement pattern and population density.

formulas.name: (1) Hunting-gathering — energy
formulas.latex: human metabolic (~2000 kcal/person/day); technology: simple tools; settlement: nomadic bands of 20–50; population density: < 1 person/km². Indian examples: Jarawa, Sentinelese (Andaman), Cholanaikkan (Kerala).

formulas.name: (2) Pastoral — energy
formulas.latex: metabolic + animal labour; technology: domesticated livestock; settlement: transhumant; density: 1–10 persons/km². Examples: Gujar Bakarwals (J&K), Gaddis (Himachal), Rabaris (Gujarat).

formulas.name: (3) Agricultural — energy
formulas.latex: metabolic + animal + biomass; technology: plough, irrigation; settlement: sedentary villages; density: 50–500 persons/km². Examples: Indo-Gangetic wheat-rice belt.

formulas.name: (4) Industrial — energy
formulas.latex: fossil-fuel + grid electricity; technology: mechanised; settlement: urban; density: > 1000 persons/km². Examples: Mumbai–Pune industrial corridor.

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: A Bakarwal household of 6 persons migrates 280 km annually between al\pine pastures (Kashmir, > 2500 m) and the Shiwalik foothills. Annual transhumant distance per person = 280 km; energy throughput per household ≈ 6 × 5 kWh/day × 365 = 10,950 kWh/yr — about 1/40th of an equivalent urban household.

formulas.name: Quantitative terms
formulas.latex: hunting-gathering, pastoral, agricultural, industrial, transhumance, domestication, Jarawa, Sentinelese, Bakarwal, Gaddi, PVTG, metabolic energy, kWh/person/day.

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 3
formulas.latex: IMPACT ON NATURAL RESOURCE BASE — ENERGY, MATERIALS, SCALE

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Impact of each mode on the natural resource base evaluated across four parameters: energy resources, material resources, scale of catchment, quantity of resources used. Throughput rises sharply from hunting-gathering to industrial.

formulas.name: Energy
formulas.latex: H-G uses only metabolic energy; pastoral adds draught animals; agricultural adds biomass (firewood, dung); industrial adds fossil fuels and electricity.

formulas.name: Materials
formulas.latex: H-G uses stone, wood, bone; pastoral adds hide, wool, milk; agricultural adds timber, brick, metal; industrial adds steel, cement, plastics, rare earths.

formulas.name: Scale of catchment
formulas.latex: H-G = local (few km²); pastoral = regional (hundreds of km²); agricultural = sub-continental; industrial = global supply chain.

formulas.name: where ρ
formulas.latex: per-ca\pita material consumption (t/person/yr), C = catchment factor (area needed per unit material, ha/t), N = population.

formulas.name: Units
formulas.latex: M in tonnes/yr; A in hectares (ha).

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: A village of N = 1000 persons uses firewood at ρ = 0.5 t/person/yr; the catchment factor for firewood from a dry-deciduous forest is C = 0.4 ha/t (sustainable yield).

formulas.name: Indian context
formulas.latex: India's per-ca\pita material consumption ≈ 5 t/yr (2022); national throughput ≈ 7 billion t/yr.

formulas.name: Quantitative terms
formulas.latex: energy resources, material resources, scale of catchment, resource throughput, fossil fuels, metabolic energy, supply chain, sustainable yield, firewood, dry-deciduous forest.

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 4
formulas.latex: ECOLOGICAL IMPACT — LAND TRANSFORMATION, HABITAT, BIODIVERSITY

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Ecological impacts of each mode: H-G causes minimal land modification; pastoral induces grazing-driven vegetation change; agricultural transforms land via clearing, ploughing, monoculture; industrial causes large-scale land transformation, habitat fragmentation, biogeochemical-cycle disruption and climate modification.

formulas.name: where C_i
formulas.latex: annual consumption of resource i (kg/yr), Y_i = national-average yield for i (kg/ha/yr), EFi = equivalence factor for land type of i (dimensionless).

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: An Indian urban resident consumes C_cereals = 150 kg/yr (Y = 2700 kg/ha/yr, cropland EF = 2.5) and C_firewood = 250 kg/yr (Y = 1200 kg/ha/yr, forest EF = 1.3).

formulas.name: Quantitative terms
formulas.latex: ecological footprint, biocapacity, ecological deficit, land transformation, habitat fragmentation, monoculture, greenhouse gases, global hectare, equivalence factor.

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 5
formulas.latex: SOCIAL ORGANISATION — GROUP SIZE, KINSHIP, DIVISION OF LABOUR

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Social organisation across the four modes, examined through group size, kinship, division of labour, and man-nature relationship.

formulas.name: Group size
formulas.latex: H-G bands 20–50; pastoral bands/tribes 100–500; agricultural villages 500–5000; industrial cities 10⁵–10⁷.

formulas.name: Kinship
formulas.latex: H-G bilateral; pastoral patrilineal; agricultural patrilineal + nuclear family; industrial bilateral nuclear.

formulas.name: Division of labour
formulas.latex: H-G age-sex only; pastoral age-sex + herding; agricultural occupational specialisation (smith, potter, carpenter); industrial complex occupational specialisation.

formulas.name: Property
formulas.latex: H-G communal; pastoral communal-herd + private-animal; agricultural private-land; industrial private-ca\pital.

Worked example
formulas.latex: For agricultural mode (m = 3): log10(G) ≈ 1.3 + 0.7(2) = 2.7 → G ≈ 500, matching a ty\pical Indian village. For industrial (m = 4): log10(G) ≈ 3.4 → G ≈ 2500 (city ward), consistent with the layered structure of urban society.

formulas.name: Quantitative terms
formulas.latex: band, tribe, chiefdom, bilateral kinship, patrilineal, nuclear family, occupational specialisation, communal access, private property, Dunbar's number, Jarawa.

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 6
formulas.latex: IDEOLOGY AND MAN-NATURE RELATIONSHIP — CASE STUDIES

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Ideology (the conceptual framework) and idiom (its cultural expression) of the man-nature relationship across the four modes.

formulas.name: H-G
formulas.latex: animism, totemism — humans as part of nature; reverence for game animals and sacred groves. Example: Mawphlang sacred grove (Meghalaya) protected by Khasi taboo for > 700 years.

formulas.name: Pastoral
formulas.latex: nature as provider; cyclical view tied to seasons and pastures; Quranic and Vedic references to cattle as wealth.

formulas.name: Agricultural
formulas.latex: nature as cultivable partner; earth as mother (Bhumi, Prithvi); festivals of gratitude (Pongal, Bihu, Onam).

formulas.name: Industrial
formulas.latex: nature as resource/commodity; commodification of land, water, genes; dominance ethic (Baconian).

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: A Khasi clan harvests 1 m³ of sacred-grove wood only for funeral rites (subsistence_value ≈ ₹500 ritual equivalent). The same 1 m³ of teak sold in a sawmill fetches ₹35,000. CI = (35000 − 500)/500 = 69 → highly commodified in the industrial mode.

formulas.name: Quantitative terms
formulas.latex: ideology, idiom, animism, totemism, commodification, sacred grove, Mawphlang, Khasi, Bhumi, Pongal, Baconian dominance ethic.

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 7
formulas.latex: ECOLOGICAL CONFLICTS FROM COEXISTENCE OF MODES

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Conflicts arising when different modes of existence occupy the same landscape. Types: (a) land-use conflict (industry vs agriculture vs forest); (b) water conflict (industry vs irrigation vs drinking); (c) forest-resource conflict (tribal vs state vs industry); (d) displacement and marginalisation of weaker modes.

formulas.name: Indian examples
formulas.latex: Niyamgiri (Odisha) — Dongria Kondh (H-G/tribal) vs Vedanta bauxite mining; Plachimada (Kerala) — Coca-Cola groundwater extraction vs local farmers; Sardar Sarovar Dam (Narmada) — industrial/agricultural water vs adivasi displacement; POSCO (Odisha) — steel plant vs betel-vine agriculturists.

formulas.name: where D
formulas.latex: direct violence (0–10), S = structural violence (0–10), I = institutional/cultural violence (0–10).

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: Niyamgiri case — D = 4 (police action), S = 8 (displacement threat), I = 7 (cultural marginalisation). CI = (4+8+7)/3 = 6.3 (high). The 2013 Supreme Court gram-sabha ruling reduced S to 3 → CI = (4+3+7)/3 = 4.7 (moderate) after community consent was made mandatory.

formulas.name: Quantitative terms
formulas.latex: ecological conflict, land-use conflict, water conflict, displacement, marginalisation, Niyamgiri, Dongria Kondh, Plachimada, Sardar Sarovar, adivasi, gram sabha, structural violence.

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 8
formulas.latex: ECOSYSTEM CONCEPT — STRUCTURE, BIOTIC AND ABIOTIC COMPONENTS

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Ecology (Haeckel 1866) = scientific study of interactions between organisms and their environment. Ecosystem (Tansley 1935) = self-sustaining functional unit where biotic and abiotic components interact through energy flow and nutrient cycling.

formulas.name: Biotic components
formulas.latex: producers (autotrophs — green plants, cyanobacteria, chemosynthetic bacteria), consumers (primary/herbivores, secondary/carnivores, tertiary/apex, omnivores), decomposers (saprotrophs — fungi, bacteria; detritivores — earthworms, termites).

formulas.name: Abiotic components
formulas.latex: climatic (light, temperature, humidity, wind), edaphic (soil texture, pH, moisture), topographic (altitude, slope), and inorganic substances (C, N, P, H₂O, CO₂).

formulas.name: Ecosystem types
formulas.latex: natural (forest, grassland, desert, pond, ocean) vs artificial (crop field, aquarium, dam); terrestrial vs aquatic.

formulas.name: where N
formulas.latex: number of individuals, w̄ = mean dry biomass per individual.

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: In a 1 m² quadrat of a deciduous forest (Palamu, Jharkhand), 4 sal saplings of mean dry weight 2.5 kg each are counted.

formulas.name: Quantitative terms

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 9
formulas.latex: TROPHIC RELATIONSHIPS — FOOD CHAINS, FOOD WEBS, BIOMAGNIFICATION

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Food chain = linear sequence of organisms through which energy flows. Grazing food chain (GFC): producer → herbivore → carnivore → apex (e.g., grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk). Detritus food chain (DFC): dead organic matter → detritivore → predator (e.g., leaf litter → earthworm → frog). Food web = interconnected network of food chains in an ecosystem. Trophic levels: producer (TL1), primary consumer (TL2), secondary (TL3), tertiary (TL4), apex (TL5).

formulas.name: Biomagnification
formulas.latex: increasing concentration of a persistent, fat-soluble toxin along trophic levels. Bioaccumulation = build-up within a single organism over its lifetime.

formulas.name: Energy available at trophic level n
formulas.latex: E_n = E_0 × (0.10)**(n−1), where E_0 = energy fixed by producers.

formulas.name: Units
formulas.latex: energy in kJ/m²/yr; concentration in mg/kg (ppm, wet weight).

formulas.name: Worked example (energy)
formulas.latex: A Sundarbans mangrove fixes E_0 = 20,000 kJ/m²/yr. Energy reaching:

formulas.latex: DDT in Lake Kariba — water 0.003 ppm → phytoplankton 0.04 ppm → zooplankton 0.25 ppm → small fish 1.2 ppm → large fish 4.0 ppm → fish-eating bird 24 ppm.

formulas.name: Indian context
formulas.latex: DDT was banned for agriculture in India in 1989 but is still used under vector-control programmes; eggshell thinning reported in Sarus cranes.

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 10
formulas.latex: RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN ORGANISMS — COMPETITION, PREDATION, MUTUALISM, PARASITISM

formulas.name: Mutualism — both species benefit (obligate symbiosis or facultative). Examples
formulas.latex: Rhizobium–legume (N₂ fixation), lichen (fungus + alga/cyanobacterium), mycorrhizae, fig–fig wasp, coral–zooxanthellae.

formulas.latex: population sizes; K₁, K₂ = carrying capacities; α, β = competition coefficients (effect of one species on the other expressed in units of the first species).

formulas.name: Outcome
formulas.latex: species 1 wins if K₁/α > K₂ and K₂/β < K₁; coexistence if K₁/α > K₂ and K₂/β > K₁.

formulas.name: Result

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 11
formulas.latex: HABITATS AND NICHES — GAUSE'S COMPETITIVE EXCLUSION PRINCIPLE

formulas.name: Habitat
formulas.latex: the physical place where an organism lives (forest, pond, desert, estuary).

formulas.name: Ecological niche (Hutchinson 1957)
formulas.latex: the full functional role and position of a species, including its tolerance ranges for all abiotic factors and its biotic interactions. Fundamental niche = the niche in the absence of competitors/predators; realised niche = the actual niche occu\pied in the presence of biotic constraints (smaller subset).

formulas.name: Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle (1934)
formulas.latex: two species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely; one will exclude the other. Resolution mechanisms: resource partitioning (sub-dividing a shared resource) and character displacement (evolutionary divergence of traits).

formulas.name: Classic experiment
formulas.latex: Paramecium aurelia and P. caudatum grown together → P. aurelia outcompetes P. caudatum because they share the same realised niche.

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 12
formulas.latex: FLOW OF ENERGY — PHOTOSYNTHETIC, TROPHIC, ASSIMILATION EFFICIENCIES

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Energy flow is unidirectional (sun → producers → consumers → decomposers) and obeys the laws of thermodynamics. Only ~1–2% of incident solar radiation is captured as gross primary productivity (GPP); the rest is reflected, transmitted, or lost as heat.

formulas.name: Trophic efficiency (TE)
formulas.latex: (production at level n+1) / (production at level n) × 100 — ty\pically 5–20%, average ~10% (Lindeman).

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: A tro\pical wet-evergreen forest (Silent Valley, Kerala) receives PAR = 2.5 × 10⁶ kJ/m²/yr; GPP = 45,000 kJ/m²/yr; res\piration R = 25,000 kJ/m²/yr.

formulas.name: Trophic transfer to herbivores (TE
formulas.latex: 10%): P_herb = 2,000 kJ/m²/yr; to carnivores = 200; to apex = 20 — matching the inverted energy pyramid (always upright).

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 13
formulas.latex: NUTRIENT CYCLES — CARBON AND NITROGEN CYCLES

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Biogeochemical cycles move elements between reservoir pool (large, slow exchange), exchange pool (smaller, dynamic), and biotic community. Generalised model: uptake → transfer through food chain → return via decomposition.

formulas.name: Carbon cycle
formulas.latex: reservoirs = ocean (≈ 38,000 Gt C), fossil fuels (≈ 5,000–10,000 Gt C), atmosphere (≈ 870 Gt C as CO₂, ~420 ppm in 2024), terrestrial biomass (≈ 550 Gt C), soils (≈ 1,500 Gt C). Processes: photosynthesis (uptake), res\piration (release), combustion (release), decomposition, ocean–atmosphere exchange, weathering, sedimentation (long-term sink as carbonate rock).

formulas.name: Nitrogen cycle
formulas.latex: reservoir = atmosphere (N₂, 78% of air, ≈ 4 × 10⁹ Gt N). Steps: nitrogen fixation (N₂ → NH₃) by Rhizobium (legume root nodules), Azotobacter (free-living), Cyanobacteria (Anabaena in rice paddies), and industrial Haber–Bosch (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, ~450 °C, 200 atm); nitrification (NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ by Nitrosomonas; NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻ by Nitrobacter); assimilation by plants; ammonification (organic N → NH₄⁺) by decomposers; denitrification (NO₃⁻ → N₂) by Pseudomonas denitrificans under anaerobic conditions.

formulas.name: Residence time (τ)
formulas.latex: Reservoir mass (M) / Flux in or out (F)

formulas.name: Units
formulas.latex: M in Gt (gigatonnes = 10⁹ t), F in Gt/yr, τ in years.

formulas.name: Worked example (carbon residence)
formulas.latex: Atmospheric CO₂ reservoir M ≈ 870 Gt C; net flux from fossil-fuel + land-use change F ≈ 11 Gt C/yr (2023).

formulas.name: Worked example (nitrogen fixation)
formulas.latex: A rice paddy in Tamil Nadu hosts Anabaena fixing 30 kg N/ha/season; with two seasons, annual fixation = 60 kg N/ha — replacing ~130 kg of urea (46% N), saving ~₹2,600/ha in fertiliser cost.

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 15
formulas.latex: DISRUPTION OF NUTRIENT CYCLES AND HABITATS

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Human activities disrupt biogeochemical cycles and habitats.

formulas.name: Carbon cycle disruption
formulas.latex: fossil-fuel combustion raised atmospheric CO₂ from ~280 ppm (pre-industrial 1750) to ~420 ppm (2024); ocean absorbs ~30% of emitted CO₂ → carbonic acid → ocean acidification (pH dropped from 8.21 to 8.05 since 1750, a 30% increase in H⁺).

formulas.name: Nitrogen cycle disruption
formulas.latex: Haber–Bosch fixation now exceeds natural terrestrial fixation (~210 Gt N/yr anthropogenic vs ~140 natural); excess nitrate → eutrophication, algal blooms, dead zones (Gulf of Mexico dead zone ~15,000 km² in 2023; Indian dead zones off the Kerala coast and in Chilika lake e\pisodic).

formulas.name: Ozone depletion
formulas.latex: CFCs release Cl radicals → catalytic O₃ destruction; Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out CFCs; ozone hole over Antarctica is recovering (~25 million km² in 2022 vs 28 million km² peak).

formulas.name: Habitat destruction/fragmentation
formulas.latex: India lost ~1.6 million ha of forest between 2001 and 2023 (Global Forest Watch). Invasive species: Lantana camara (now in > 40% of Indian forests), water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes), Parthenium hysterophorus.

formulas.name: Acid rain threshold
formulas.latex: pH < 5.6 (pure water in equilibrium with atmospheric CO₂ ≈ 5.6).

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: A rain sample near a thermal power plant (Singrauli, MP) has [H⁺] = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L.

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 16
formulas.latex: POLLUTION CONTROL APPROACHES — PREVENTION AND CONTROL

formulas.name: Prevention
formulas.latex: source reduction — eliminate or reduce pollutant generation at source. Tools: fuel substitution (low-S coal, CNG), process modification (closed-loop, dry processing), cleaner production, green chemistry, material substitution.

formulas.name: Control
formulas.latex: end-of-\pipe treatment — capture/treat pollutant after generation but before release. Tools: scrubbers (flue-gas desulphurisation), electrostatic preci\pitators (ESP), catalytic converters, effluent treatment plants (ETP), sewage treatment plants (STP), bag-houses.

formulas.latex: WTO (1995, successor to GATT) governs global trade. Disputes: US–Mexico tuna-dolphin case (1991); Shrimp–Turtle case (1998, India was a respondent).

formulas.name: PHI

formulas.name: Hi-tech
formulas.latex: ca\pital-intensive, high-energy, automated, centralised — nuclear reactors, supersonic aircraft, supercomputers, AI data centres. High skill, high throughput, high environmental footprint per unit ca\pital.

formulas.name: Low-tech / traditional
formulas.latex: labour-intensive, low-energy, decentralised — bullock-cart, hand-pump, chulha, draft-animal plough. Low throughput, low skill, often low efficiency.

formulas.latex: between traditional and modern; uses modern knowledge but small-scale, affordable, locally maintainable — e.g., pedal-powered water pumps, improved chulha (LPG-stove replacement), micro-hydro, biogas.

formulas.name: Appropriate technology
formulas.latex: technology suited to the environmental, cultural, social and economic context — not necessarily low-tech; criteria: (i) uses local resources, (ii) locally repairable, (iii) environmentally benign, (iv) socially equitable, (v) economically viable. Examples: Aravind Eye Care (high-tech but appropriate), Jaipur Foot, TARA baler, biogas (DESL/ARTI), solar lanterns (TERA, d.light).

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 26
formulas.latex: ECOSYSTEM ANALYSIS — COMPLEX SYSTEMS, CRITICAL VARIABLES

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Ecosystems are complex adaptive systems with emergent properties (properties of the whole not predictable from parts), feedback loops (negative/stabilising and positive/amplifying), thresholds (tip\ping points), and non-linear dynamics. Examples of thresholds: lake eutrophication (clear → turbid at a critical P loading), coral bleaching (above DHW 4), forest dieback above a warming threshold.

formulas.name: Critical variables
formulas.latex: state variables that, if pushed past a threshold, flip the ecosystem to an alternative stable state. Examples: phosphorus in lakes, herbivore biomass in savanna (grassland ↔ shrubland), sea-ice extent in Arctic, groundwater table in Punjab (rice-wheat zone — water table falling ~0.5 m/yr).

formulas.name: System indicators (measurable surrogates of ecosystem health)
formulas.latex: primary productivity (NDVI from satellites), dissolved oxygen, species richness, Shannon diversity index, BOD, soil organic carbon, faunal bio-indicators.

formulas.name: Resilience
formulas.latex: capacity to absorb disturbance and reorganise while retaining function; hysteresis = delayed or irreversible recovery after disturbance.

formulas.name: where p_i
formulas.latex: proportion of individuals in species i (n_i / N). H' ranges 0 (single species) to ln(S) (max evenness with S species).

formulas.latex: D = 1 − Σ p_i²  (probability two random individuals are different species)

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Tension between "quantity of life" (population, GDP, resource consumption, material prosperity) and "quality of environment" (clean air, water, soil, biodiversity, ecosystem services, health, equity).

formulas.name: Quantity indicators
formulas.latex: GDP (India ~$3.9 trillion 2024), GDP per ca\pita (~$2,800), population (1.43 billion, 2024 — world's most populous), per-ca\pita energy use (~18 kWh/day), material footprint (~5 t/ca\pita).

formulas.name: Quality indicators
formulas.latex: AQI (Delhi annual PM2.5 ~100 µg/m³, ~10× WHO guideline), water quality (only ~50% of rivers fit for bathing, CPCB 2022), forest cover (~21.7% of geographic area, ISFR 2021), species at risk (~1,400 species on IUCN Red List from India), Human Development Index (India 0.644, rank 134/193, 2024).

formulas.name: Trade-offs
formulas.latex: GDP growth vs emissions (India's emission intensity fell 35% between 2005 and 2022 — relative decoupling; absolute emissions still rising). Decoupling strategies: circular economy, renewable energy, energy efficiency, dematerialisation, sustainable consumption.

formulas.name: Ecosystem services (MEA 2005)
formulas.latex: provisioning (food, fibre, water, genetic resources), regulating (climate, flood, disease, pollination), cultural (recreation, s\piritual, aesthetic), supporting (nutrient cycling, soil formation, primary production). India's ecosystem services valued at ~$1.7 trillion/yr (TERI estimate).

formulas.latex: environmental impact, P = population, A = affluence (per-ca\pita consumption = GDP/P), T = technology (impact per unit consumption = emissions/GDP).

formulas.name: Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI) adjustment
formulas.latex: GPI = C_adj + household work + services of ca\pital − income inequality − pollution − resource depletion − crime − family breakdown.

formulas.name: I_2022/I_2005
formulas.latex: 1.27 × 3.0 × 0.65 = 2.48 → environmental impact ~2.5× higher (consistent with CO₂ emissions rising from ~1.3 to ~2.8 Gt).

formulas.name: FORMULA SET 28
formulas.latex: DESIGN OF SOLUTIONS — GENERATING OPTIONS, LATERAL THINKING

formulas.name: Key relationships
formulas.latex: Design of solutions for environmental problems requires both structured (analytical) and creative (generative) thinking.

formulas.name: Blocks in thinking
formulas.latex: functional fixedness (seeing objects only in their usual function), mental set (persisting with previously successful strategies), confirmation bias (seeking evidence that confirms pre-existing beliefs), anchoring, availability heuristic, framing effects, groupthink.

formulas.name: Convergent tools

formulas.latex: POST-HARVEST PRACTICES — FOOD PROCESSING AND PRESERVATION

formulas.name: Safe storage MC
formulas.latex: wheat ≤ 12 %, rice ≤ 13 %, pulses ≤ 10 %, oilseeds ≤ 7–8 %; above ⇒ mould (Aspergillus aflatoxin risk, B1 limit 30 µg/kg IS 7497).

formulas.name: Equilibrium moisture content EMC
formulas.latex: f(RH, T); below 65 % RH safe for most grains.

formulas.name: MR
formulas.latex: (M − M_e)/(M_0 − M_e) = e**(−k·t); k ~ 0.1–1 h⁻¹ depending on T, airflow.

formulas.name: Pasteurisation
formulas.latex: milk 63 °C × 30 min (LTLT) or 72 °C × 15 s (HTST); achieves 5-log reduction in pathogens (Coxiella burnetii target).

formulas.name: F₀ value (12-D process for Clostridium botulinum)
formulas.latex: F₀ = 10**((T − 121.1)/z) × t; z = 10 °C; F₀ ≥ 3 min for low-acid canned foods.

formulas.name: D_T
formulas.latex: time for 1-log reduction at temperature T; z = temperature rise for 10× change in D.

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: D_121 = 0.2 min for C. botulinum spores; for 12-log reduction need 12 × 0.2 = 2.4 min ⇒ F₀ ≈ 2.4 min (≈ 3 min standard).

formulas.latex: NATURAL RESOURCE ECONOMICS — RESOURCES, SCARCITY, ACCOUNTING

formulas.name: Renewable (flow)
formulas.latex: solar, wind, hydro, biomass — regeneration > extraction.

formulas.name: Conditionally renewable
formulas.latex: groundwater, fish, forests — extraction ≤ regeneration else "open access" tragedy.

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: India coal reserves ≈ 3.6×10¹¹ t (Geological Survey), production ~1.0×10⁹ t/yr (2023-24) ⇒ R/P ≈ 360 yr (but extractable much less). India petroleum R/P ≈ 18 yr; natural gas ≈ 40 yr.

formulas.name: • Physical scarcity
formulas.latex: per-ca\pita availability < 1000 m³/yr water (water-stressed < 1700). India per-ca\pita water 1486 m³/yr (2021) ⇒ water-stressed; projected 1140 by 2050.

formulas.name: • Economic scarcity
formulas.latex: price relative to income; affordability index.

formulas.name: Depletion
formulas.latex: (P_resource − C_extraction − normal return on produced ca\pital) × Q_extracted.

formulas.name: India
formulas.latex: ENVIS \pilot in 8 states; CSoE 2024 estimates environmental costs ≈ 5–7 % of GDP.

formulas.name: 6. Hartwick rule
formulas.latex: invest resource rents (R_t) in reproducible ca\pital so that dK_total/dt ≥ 0 ⇒ constant consumption ⇒ weak sustainability.

formulas.latex: natural resource economics, renewable/non-renewable, stock/flow, scarcity, R/P ratio, Hotelling's rule, Malthusian theory, limits to growth, SEEA, depletion, green NDP, Hartwick rule.

formulas.latex: GNP VS OTHER MEASURES — NET ECONOMIC WELFARE, NATURAL CAPITAL

formulas.name: 1. GDP (income approach)
formulas.latex: W + R + i + PR (wages + rents + interest + profits).

formulas.name: GNP
formulas.latex: GDP + NFIA (net factor income from abroad).

formulas.name: NEW
formulas.latex: NNP + non-market benefits (leisure, household work, volunteer) − regrettable/negative items (commuting, pollution cleanup, crime control, environmental damage).

formulas.name: GPI
formulas.latex: Personal consumption weighted by income distribution

formulas.name: 5. Gross National Happiness (GNH, Bhutan, 1972 — 4 pillars, 9 domains, 33 indicators)
formulas.latex: psychological wellbeing, health, education, time-use, cultural diversity, good governance, community vitality, ecological diversity, living standards. GNH Index = weighted sufficiency score across domains.

formulas.name: K_natural
formulas.latex: non-renewable stocks + renewable stocks + land + ecosystems.

formulas.name: 7. Inclusive Wealth Index (IWI, UN-IHDP)
formulas.latex: W = Σ (K_man + K_human + K_natural) × shadow prices; India IWI growth 0.4 %/yr 1990-2010 vs GDP 5–6 % ⇒ wealth growing far slower than GDP (depletion of natural ca\pital offsets human-ca\pital gains).

formulas.latex: GNP, GDP, NNP, NEW, natural ca\pital, ecological ca\pital, GPI, GNH, IWI, environmental ^{\circ}radation, non-market transactions, depreciation of natural ca\pital, ecosystem services, Samuelson, Nordhaus, shadow prices.

formulas.name: t*

formulas.name: 3. Coase theorem
formulas.latex: with well-defined property rights and zero transaction costs, private bargaining yields efficient outcome regardless of initial allocation; in practice transaction costs and many-affected parties limit applicability (e.g. Delhi air pollution).

formulas.name: Decision rule
formulas.latex: NPV > 0 and BCR > 1 ⇒ accept; choose highest NPV among mutually exclusive.

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: A check-dam project, life 30 yr, r = 8 %.

formulas.name: 5. Social discount rate
formulas.latex: India MoSPI recommends 8 % (with sensitivity 5 %, 10 %); declining for long horizons (climate, ≥ 50 yr) per Stern vs Nordhaus debate.

formulas.latex: WTP/WTA from surveys; e.g. WTP for Taj Trapezium clean air ~₹150/household/month.

formulas.name: • Hedonic pricing
formulas.latex: property price = f(air quality, noise, view, distance to park).

formulas.latex: include EC and EB; distributional weights for poor vs rich (Atkinson weighting).

formulas.name: ToT
formulas.latex: (Index of export prices / Index of import prices) × 100.

formulas.name: 2. Pollution Haven Hypothesis (PHH)
formulas.latex: trade liberalisation relocates dirty industries to countries with weak regulation.

formulas.name: PHH index
formulas.latex: (pollution-intensive exports of low-regulation country) / (total pollution-intensive world exports).

formulas.name: Empirical
formulas.latex: China 2002-2010 absorbed ~20 % of OECD dirty exports; India leather/tannery, textile-dyeing clusters (Tiruppur, Kanpur) reflect PHH + race to the bottom.

formulas.name: Leakage (%)
formulas.latex: (emissions increase abroad due to domestic policy) / (emissions reduced domestically) × 100.

formulas.name: Formula
formulas.latex: Growth Rate (%) = [(Population at end - Population at start) / Population at start] x 100

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: India population 2001 = 1,028 million. 2011 = 1,210 million. Growth rate = [(1,210 - 1,028) / 1,028] x 100 = 17.7% over 10 years. Annual growth rate = 17.7 / 10 = 1.77% per year (decadal growth was 17.7%).

formulas.name: Formula
formulas.latex: Natural Growth Rate (%) = (Birth Rate - Death Rate) / 10

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: India CBR = 17.1, CDR = 6.4. Natural growth rate = (17.1 - 6.4) / 10 = 1.07% per year.

formulas.name: Variables

formulas.latex: If a station has mean rainfall 1,000 mm and standard deviation 200 mm, CV = (200 / 1,000) x 100 = 20%. High CV (>25%) indicates unreliable rainfall (drought-prone). Low CV (<15%) indicates reliable rainfall.

formulas.name: Worked example
formulas.latex: If net sown area = 100 ha and gross cropped area = 150 ha (50 ha double-cropped), crop\ping intensity = (150 / 100) x 100 = 150%. Higher crop\ping intensity indicates more intensive land use (requires irrigation).

formulas.name: Efficiency

formulas.name: Median

formulas.name: Limit Comparison Test
formulas.latex: \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = c \in (0,\infty) \implies \sum a_n \text{ and } \sum b_n \text{ converge or diverge together}

formulas.name: Lebesgue Dominated Convergence Theorem
formulas.latex: f_n \to f \text{ a.e.}, \ |f_n| \leq g \in L^1 \implies \lim_{n\to\infty} \int f_n\,d\mu = \int f\,d\mu

formulas.name: Cauchy-Riemann Equations
formulas.latex: \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y},\quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}

formulas.name: Morera's Theorem
formulas.latex: \oint_{\gamma} f(z)\,dz = 0 \text{ for all closed } \gamma \implies f \text{ is analytic}

formulas.name: Rouché's Theorem
formulas.latex: |f(z) - g(z)| < |g(z)| \text{ on } \gamma \implies f,g \text{ have same number of zeros inside } \gamma

formulas.name: Liouville's Theorem
formulas.latex: f \text{ entire and bounded} \implies f \text{ is constant}

formulas.name: Maximum Modulus Principle
formulas.latex: |f(z)| \leq \max_{\partial D} |f| \text{ for } f \text{ analytic on bounded domain } D

formulas.name: Singular Value Decomposition
formulas.latex: A = U\Sigma V^T,\quad U^TU = I,\ V^TV = I,\ \Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r)

formulas.name: QR Decomposition via Gram-Schmidt
formulas.latex: A = QR,\quad Q^TQ = I,\ R \text{ upper triangular}

formulas.name: LU Decomposition
formulas.latex: PA = LU,\quad P \text{ permutation},\ L \text{ lower triangular},\ U \text{ upper triangular}

formulas.name: Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization
formulas.latex: u_k = v_k - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \frac{\langle v_k, u_j \rangle}{\langle u_j, u_j \rangle} u_j

formulas.name: Givens Rotation
formulas.latex: G(i,j,\theta) = I \text{ except } 2\times2 \text{ rotation in } (i,j) \text{ plane}

formulas.name: Gaussian Elimination
formulas.latex: Ux = c \text{ after forward elimination, then back substitution}

formulas.name: Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient
formulas.latex: x_{k+1} = x_k + \alpha_k p_k,\quad p_{k+1} = -\nabla f(x_{k+1}) + \beta_k p_k

formulas.name: Convex Set Definition
formulas.latex: (1-t)x + ty \in C \text{ for all } x,y \in C,\ t \in [0,1]

formulas.name: Subgradient Definition
formulas.latex: f(y) \geq f(x) + g^T(y-x) \text{ for all } y \implies g \in \partial f(x)

formulas.name: Christoffel Symbols of the First Kind
Christoffel Symbols of the Second Kind
Classification of Second-Order PDEs
formulas.latex: A\phi_{xx} + 2B\phi_{xy} + C\phi_{yy} + \cdots: \begin{cases} B^2 - AC < 0 & \text{elliptic} \\ B^2 - AC = 0 & \text{parabolic} \\ B^2 - AC > 0 & \text{hyperbolic} \end{cases}

formulas.name: Ring Ideal Definition
formulas.latex: I \triangleleft R: I+I \subseteq I,\ R\cdot I \subseteq I

formulas.name: Submodule Definition
formulas.latex: N \leq M: rn \in N \text{ for all } r \in R,\ n \in N

formulas.name: Open Set Definition (Metric Space)
formulas.latex: U \text{ open} \iff \forall x \in U,\ \exists\epsilon > 0: B_\epsilon(x) \subseteq U

formulas.name: Heine-Borel Theorem
formulas.latex: K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \text{ compact} \iff K \text{ closed and bounded}

formulas.name: Connectedness
formulas.latex: \text{No separation } U,V: X=U\cup V,\ U\cap V=\emptyset,\ U,V \text{ open nonempty}

formulas.name: Product Topology Basis
formulas.latex: \mathcal{B} = \{U \times V : U \text{ open in } X,\ V \text{ open in } Y\}

formulas.name: Quotient Topology
formulas.latex: U \subseteq X/\sim \text{ open} \iff \pi^{-1}(U) \text{ open in } X

formulas.name: Hausdorff Space
formulas.latex: \forall x \neq y,\ \exists U,V \text{ open}: x \in U,\ y \in V,\ U \cap V = \emptyset

formulas.name: Urysohn Lemma
formulas.latex: X \text{ normal},\ A,B \text{ closed disjoint} \implies \exists f: X \to [0,1],\ f|_A=0,\ f|_B=1

formulas.name: Divisibility by 2
formulas.latex: n \equiv 0 \pmod{2} \iff \text{last digit of } n \text{ is even}

formulas.name: Divisibility by 5
formulas.latex: n \equiv 0 \pmod{5} \iff \text{last digit of } n \text{ is 0 or 5}

formulas.name: Sum of First n Natural Numbers
Sum of Squares of First n Natural Numbers
Sum of Cubes of First n Natural Numbers
Chinese Remainder Theorem
formulas.latex: x \equiv a_i \pmod{n_i} \quad \text{has unique solution modulo } N = \prod n_i \text{ if } \gcd(n_i, n_j)=1

formulas.name: System of Two Linear Equations
formulas.latex: \begin{cases} a_1x + b_1y = c_1 \\ a_2x + b_2y = c_2 \end{cases}

formulas.name: Sum and Product of Quadratic Roots (Vieta)
Quartic Formula (Ferrari)
formulas.latex: \text{Solution of } ax^4 + bx^3 + cx^2 + dx + e = 0 \text{ by Ferrari's method}

formulas.name: Polynomial Remainder Theorem
formulas.latex: P(x) \text{ divided by } (x-a) \text{ leaves remainder } P(a)

formulas.name: Factor Theorem
formulas.latex: (x-a) \text{ is a factor of } P(x) \iff P(a) = 0

formulas.name: Arithmetic Progression - Sum of n Terms
Geometric Progression - Sum of n Terms
Multinomial Theorem
formulas.latex: (x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_m)^n = \sum \frac{n!}{n_1!n_2!\cdots n_m!} x_1^{n_1} x_2^{n_2} \cdots x_m^{n_m}

formulas.name: Permutations with Identical Items
formulas.latex: P_{ident}(n; n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k) = \frac{n!}{n_1! n_2! \cdots n_k!}

formulas.name: Pigeonhole Principle
formulas.latex: \text{If } n \text{ items in } m \text{ boxes and } n > m, \text{ then } \geq 1 \text{ box has } \geq 2 \text{ items}

formulas.name: Complex Number - Polar Form
formulas.latex: z = r(\cos \theta + i\sin \theta) = re^{i\theta}, \quad r = |z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}

formulas.name: Matrix Inverse (2x2)
formulas.latex: A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc} \begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{for } A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}

formulas.name: Determinant of 2x2 Matrix
formulas.latex: \det\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bc

formulas.name: Cross Product (3D)
formulas.latex: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ a_x & a_y & a_z \\ b_x & b_y & b_z \end{vmatrix}

formulas.name: Scalar Triple Product
formulas.latex: \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \begin{vmatrix} a_x & a_y & a_z \\ b_x & b_y & b_z \\ c_x & c_y & c_z \end{vmatrix}

formulas.name: Absolute Value Inequality
formulas.latex: |x - a| < b \iff a - b < x < a + b

formulas.name: Linear Diophantine Equation
formulas.latex: ax + by = c \text{ has integer solutions } \iff \gcd(a,b) | c

formulas.name: Squeeze Theorem
formulas.latex: g(x) \leq f(x) \leq h(x) \text{ and } \lim g(x) = \lim h(x) = L \implies \lim f(x) = L

formulas.name: Rolle's Theorem
formulas.latex: \text{If } f \text{ is continuous on } [a,b], \text{ differentiable on } (a,b), \text{ and } f(a)=f(b), \text{ then } \exists c \in (a,b) : f'(c) = 0

formulas.name: Lagrange Mean Value Theorem
formulas.latex: \text{If } f \text{ is continuous on } [a,b] \text{ and differentiable on } (a,b), \text{ then } \exists c \in (a,b) : f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}
